easy.text: What do we call the process where one cell divides to produce two identical daughter cells?

options.feedback: Correct -- mitosis produces two genetically identical cells.
Meiosis produces four genetically different sex cells, not two identical ones.
Osmosis is the movement of water across a membrane, unrelated to cell division.
Digestion breaks down food, it has nothing to do with a cell dividing.

medium.text: During which phase of mitosis do the chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell?

options.feedback: Correct -- 'meta' refers to the middle, where chromosomes align before separating.
In prophase, chromosomes are condensing but haven't lined up in the middle yet.
In anaphase, the chromosomes are already being pulled apart toward opposite ends.
In telophase, two new nuclei are forming at opposite ends of the cell.

hard.text: Which TWO of the following are phases of mitosis itself?

options.feedback: Correct -- one of the four true phases of mitosis.
Correct -- the phase where sister chromatids are pulled apart.
Interphase is the growth/DNA-replication stage that happens BEFORE mitosis starts, not a phase of mitosis itself.
Meiosis I belongs to a completely different kind of division that produces sex cells.
Cytokinesis is the splitting of the cytoplasm that follows mitosis, technically a separate process.

easy.hard: This process results in two cells with identical genetic material, unlike its close cousin that makes four different sex cells.
easy.medium: This is the type of cell division most cells in your body use to grow and repair themselves.
easy.easy: This is how one cell becomes two identical copies of itself.

medium.hard: This is the phase where the cell's already-condensed genetic material aligns itself right at the cell's equator before being pulled apart.
medium.medium: Picture chromosomes lining up in a single file down the middle of the cell -- what's this stage called?
medium.easy: This is the stage where the chromosomes gather in the center of the cell.

hard.hard: Two of these five happen strictly within mitosis itself; the others describe the resting/growth stage before mitosis begins, division specific to sex cells, or the separate process of splitting the cytoplasm.
hard.medium: Two of the five options are true mitotic phases; the rest describe what happens before mitosis, what happens in a different kind of division, or a related-but-separate process.
hard.easy: Two of these are actual steps within mitosis -- the others happen either before mitosis starts or belong to a different process.

easy.text: In DNA, which base always pairs with Adenine?

options.feedback: Correct -- Adenine always pairs with Thymine in DNA.
Guanine pairs with Cytosine, not Adenine.
Cytosine pairs with Guanine, not Adenine.
Uracil replaces Thymine in RNA, not DNA.

medium.text: Which base pair forms three hydrogen bonds, making it slightly stronger than the other DNA base pair?

options.feedback: Correct -- G-C pairs form three hydrogen bonds, one more than A-T pairs.
A-T pairs form only two hydrogen bonds, making this pair weaker, not stronger.
These two bases don't pair with each other at all in DNA.
These two bases don't pair with each other at all in DNA.

hard.text: If one strand of DNA reads A-T-G-C, what is the base sequence of its complementary strand?

options.feedback: Correct -- each base is swapped for its fixed partner: A→T, T→A, G→C, C→G.
This is identical to the original strand, not its complement -- DNA strands are never copies of themselves.
This doesn't correctly swap each base for its fixed partner in order.
This scrambles the order rather than pairing each base correctly in place.

easy.hard: This base is the smaller, single-ring type that consistently bonds with the same partner across the entire DNA molecule.
easy.medium: This is the base that always pairs with Adenine in DNA, using two hydrogen bonds.
easy.easy: Every Adenine pairs with the same partner base every single time -- which one?

medium.hard: This pair forms one extra hydrogen bond compared to the other standard DNA base pair, making it slightly more stable.
medium.medium: One base pair uses two hydrogen bonds, the other uses three -- which pair is the stronger one?
medium.easy: Two of the four DNA bases bond more tightly together than the other two -- which pair is that?

hard.hard: Match each base to its fixed partner (A↔T, G↔C) one at a time, keeping the same left-to-right order as the original strand.
hard.medium: Swap each letter for its fixed partner, keeping the same order as the original sequence.
hard.easy: Replace each letter with its matching partner base, in the same order as given.

easy.text: What is the main function of a neuron?

options.feedback: Correct -- neurons are specialized for sending messages through the nervous system.
That's the role of adipose cells, not neurons.
Digestive enzymes are made by cells in glands like the pancreas, not neurons.
That's the job of cells in the kidneys, not neurons.

medium.text: Which part of a neuron is primarily responsible for receiving signals from other neurons?

options.feedback: Correct -- dendrites branch out to catch incoming signals from neighboring neurons.
The axon sends signals away from the cell body, the opposite job.
The myelin sheath insulates the axon to speed up signals, it doesn't receive anything.
The nucleus houses the cell's DNA and manages cell activity, but isn't the signal-receiving structure.

hard.text: What is the primary function of the myelin sheath surrounding some axons?

options.text: It insulates the axon, speeding up electrical signal transmission
options.feedback: Correct -- myelin lets signals jump between gaps, traveling much faster.

options.text: It produces the neurotransmitters used to communicate with other cells
options.feedback: Neurotransmitters are produced and stored near the axon terminal, not by the myelin sheath.

options.text: It stores the neuron's genetic information
options.feedback: Genetic information is stored in the nucleus, not in the myelin sheath.

options.text: It generates the energy the neuron uses to function
options.feedback: That's the role of mitochondria within the cell, not the myelin sheath.

easy.hard: This cell type doesn't store fat, make enzymes, or filter anything -- its entire job is carrying messages quickly.
easy.medium: This cell's job is sending and receiving electrical and chemical messages throughout the body.
easy.easy: This special cell sends messages around your body and brain.

medium.hard: This branching structure is shaped to catch incoming signals from many other cells at once, unlike the single long fiber that sends signals away.
medium.medium: This is the branch-like part of the neuron built to catch incoming messages, not send them out.
medium.easy: This part looks like tree branches and catches signals coming in.

hard.hard: This fatty coating acts like insulation on a wire, letting the electrical signal jump between gaps rather than travel continuously along the whole length.
hard.medium: This coating helps the signal travel much faster by letting it 'jump' along the axon instead of moving continuously.
hard.easy: This fatty covering helps signals zip down the neuron faster.

easy.text: What is the main job of digestive enzymes?

options.text: Breaking down food into smaller molecules
options.feedback: Correct -- enzymes chemically break large food molecules into absorbable pieces.
Storage isn't an enzyme's job -- that's more the role of the liver or fat cells.
That's more the role of stomach acid and the immune system, not digestive enzymes.
Absorption happens through the intestinal walls, not through the enzymes themselves.

medium.text: Which enzyme, found in saliva, begins breaking down starches in the mouth?

options.feedback: Correct -- salivary amylase starts breaking down starch as soon as you begin chewing.
Pepsin breaks down proteins in the stomach, not starches in the mouth.
Lipase breaks down fats, mainly later in the small intestine.
Trypsin breaks down proteins in the small intestine, not starches in the mouth.

hard.text: Which TWO of the following enzymes are involved in breaking down proteins?

options.feedback: Correct -- pepsin breaks down proteins in the acidic environment of the stomach.
Correct -- trypsin continues protein breakdown in the small intestine.
Amylase targets starches, not proteins.
Lipase targets fats, not proteins.
Lactase targets the sugar lactose, not proteins.

easy.hard: These molecules don't store, kill, or absorb anything -- they chemically cut large food molecules into smaller usable pieces.
easy.medium: These are the molecules that chemically break large food particles into smaller, absorbable pieces.
easy.easy: These help break your food down into tiny pieces your body can use.

medium.hard: This enzyme is secreted by the salivary glands and specifically targets the same type of molecule found abundantly in bread and pasta.
medium.medium: This enzyme starts working the moment food enters your mouth, targeting starchy foods specifically.
medium.easy: This is the enzyme in your spit that starts breaking down starchy foods like bread.

hard.hard: One of these two works in the highly acidic environment of the stomach; the other works in the more neutral small intestine -- both target the same type of macronutrient, just at different digestive stages.
hard.medium: Two of these five specifically target protein molecules, just in different parts of the digestive tract.
hard.easy: Two of these enzymes are protein-breakers -- one works in the stomach, one in the small intestine.

easy.text: What term describes the maximum population size an environment can sustainably support?

options.feedback: Correct -- carrying capacity is the population limit an environment's resources can sustain.
Biodiversity refers to the variety of species in an area, not a population limit.
A food chain describes feeding relationships between organisms, not a population limit.
A habitat is the place where an organism lives, not a measure of population limit.

medium.text: What typically happens to a population when it exceeds its environment's carrying capacity?

options.text: The population tends to decline due to limited resources
options.feedback: Correct -- scarce resources increase competition, causing the population to shrink back down.
Unlimited growth isn't sustainable -- resource limits eventually cause a decline.

options.text: The environment's carrying capacity automatically increases
options.feedback: Carrying capacity is set by available resources, it doesn't just rise to match population size.
Exceeding resource limits does have a real effect -- it triggers a population decline.

hard.text: Carrying capacity is best defined as a population limit set primarily by which of the following?

options.text: Available resources such as food, water, and space
options.feedback: Correct -- carrying capacity reflects the combined limits of all resources an environment provides.
Predation is only one possible limiting factor, not the full definition.
Reproduction rate affects how fast a population grows, but not the resource ceiling itself.
Random events can affect populations, but they don't define the resource-based ceiling itself.

easy.hard: This term names the ceiling an ecosystem places on how many individuals it can support long-term, not a measure of variety or a description of where something lives.
easy.medium: This is the largest population size an environment can support long-term without running out of what that population needs.
easy.easy: This is the biggest number of a species an area can support without running out of resources.

medium.hard: When numbers exceed what resources can support, competition increases and resources become scarcer, pushing the population back down rather than letting it keep climbing.
medium.medium: Resources become scarce when there are too many individuals, which tends to shrink the population back down.
medium.easy: Too many individuals means not enough resources to go around, so the population usually shrinks.

hard.hard: The best definition accounts for the full set of resources (food, water, space, etc.) an environment provides, rather than isolating just one single factor like predators or reproduction alone.
hard.medium: The most complete answer covers multiple resource types together, not just one single factor in isolation.
hard.easy: The best answer mentions several resources together (food, water, space), not just one thing by itself.
